tldr: We introduce ReactHuman, a physics-grounded benchmark that tests whether multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) can produce safe, human-like reactive actions in response to sudden physical hazards, like a falling knife or a slipping plate, within rigid-body simulation. Evaluating state-of-the-art models reveals that they mishandle hazards roughly one out of three times and judge physical properties purely by appearance, exposing critical safety issues that do not diminish with model scale.
hero_caption: An overview of the ReactHuman evaluation pipeline. Scenes are synthesized via LLM semantic planning and seed-based deterministic physics generation. Within the Genesis physics simulator, time is frozen to let the MLLM decide on an action. The generated action plan is physically executed by a humanoid robot (Unitree G1) and strictly scored across five metrics spanning three axes: reasonable, safe, and physically grounded.
overview:
Research on adopting multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) as the decision core of household robots is progressing rapidly. However, whether these models can make human-like reactive decisions in response to sudden daily hazards—such as dodging a falling knife or catching a slipping plate—has remained unmeasured. Existing physical reasoning benchmarks rely on passive visual question answering (VQA) over video, while embodied AI benchmarks focus almost exclusively on long-horizon navigation and rearrangement tasks.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose ReactHuman, the first benchmark that directly evaluates MLLMs as the brains of simulated humanoids confronting sudden hazards. After viewing a brief clip (roughly 0.6 seconds) of a hazard unfolding in simulation, time is frozen, and the MLLM outputs a structured plan specifying walking velocity and 3D hand trajectory waypoints. This plan is physically executed by a humanoid robot (Unitree G1) via a whole-body controller in the same physics simulator, allowing direct observation of physical consequences, such as successful catches or tipping over from direct impacts.

ReactHuman spans 17 event families and over 1,000 reproducible scenes, incorporating adversarial probes such as steel apples that look like harmless fruit but carry extreme mass. Evaluating seven representative MLLMs reveals that models violate safety rules in roughly one out of three hazards, completely freeze in the face of slow-moving threats, and fail to deduce true physics from observed motion when appearance contradicts it. These findings deliver a crucial takeaway for robotics: scaling up model size alone does not yield reactive physical safety.
contributions: Proposed ReactHuman, the first benchmark to evaluate human-like reactive decision-making in the face of sudden household hazards through rigid-body simulation and physical execution on a humanoid.
Built an automated scene generation pipeline capable of scaling beyond 10,000 scenes, pairing LLM-driven semantic diversity with seed-based deterministic physics parameter generation.
Designed a diagnostic five-metric suite spanning three axes—Reasonable, Safe, and Physically Grounded—cleanly separating decision mistakes, safety violations, and kinematic errors.

Evaluated seven representative MLLMs to demonstrate fundamental challenges that do not shrink with model scale, including high failure rates during avoidance, rigid behavioral dispositions, and heavy reliance on visual appearance.

sections.heading: Catching a falling knife is unacceptable: The unsolved barrier of reactive decision-making
sections.summary: Humans effortlessly catch slipping plates or dodge toppling furniture, but current MLLM evaluations cannot measure such reactive safety. This study introduces ReactHuman, a diagnostic benchmark that freezes simulation time to let an MLLM plan reactive actions, which are then physically executed by a humanoid.
sections.details:
When faced with sudden daily hazards, humans react within fractions of a second by integrating symbolic, semantic reasoning ("what is this, is it safe to touch?") with intuitive physical judgment ("where and when will it land?"). Deploying MLLMs as the decision core of domestic robots demands reactive capabilities that are safe (avoid harm), reasonable (make human-aligned choices), and physically grounded (hands actually reach the object). A robot that grabs a falling blade, or correctly decides to catch a cup but swings half a meter off-target, cannot be trusted in the real world.

Yet existing benchmarks focus either on passive multiple-choice visual question answering (VQA) over video or on deliberate, long-horizon navigation and tidying tasks. Such setups cannot tease apart whether a model misidentified the hazard, understood the danger but selected a harmful action anyway, or chose the right action but miscalculated the spatial coordinates.

ReactHuman tackles this challenge using a "Freeze-and-Predict" protocol that places the MLLM as the brain of an embodied humanoid. After receiving a brief initial observation (around 0.6 seconds) right as the hazard unfolds, time inside the simulator freezes. This eliminates API latency bias and isolates decision quality. The committed motor plan is then executed in the same physical space by a reinforcement-learning-trained whole-body controller, evaluating the model through observable physical consequences rather than static multiple-choice answers.

sections.heading: From passive physical reasoning to embodied reactive action
sections.summary: Prior physical reasoning evaluations stayed confined to video QA, while Embodied AI skewed heavily toward deliberate, long-horizon tasks. By adopting a brain-spine-body decomposition, ReactHuman isolates MLLM decision-making from low-level whole-body control while evaluating reactive safety with physical consequences.
sections.details:
### Contrasting with Physical Reasoning Benchmarks
Prior efforts like Physion, CLEVRER, and PhysBench test object motion and causal prediction, but mostly in passive VQA formats where models answer text questions or pick choices after watching videos. ReactHuman fundamentally differs: the model's output directly constitutes a safety-critical motor plan (action), and ground-truth labels are automatically and deterministically extracted from simulator physical states.

### Contrasting with Embodied AI and Humanoid Research
Environments such as Habitat, BEHAVIOR-1K, and HumanoidBench prioritize navigation, long-horizon manipulation, or low-level whole-body torque control. None evaluate immediate reactive responses to sudden physical hazards. ReactHuman introduces a "brain-spine-body" decomposition: the evaluated MLLM serves as the brain, a pre-trained whole-body controller managing balance and locomotion acts as the spinal cord, and the simulated robot acts as the body. This decouples whole-body control fidelity from MLLM cognitive competence, exposing pure decision-making as a physical interaction.

### Scene Synthesis Architecture
While frameworks like Kubric and Objaverse generate scenes with large-scale 3D assets, ReactHuman enforces a clean division of labor: an LLM handles semantic composition, while a deterministic random generator handles physical parameters via integer seeds. This simultaneously achieves broad natural-language scene variety and bit-for-bit reproducibility with exact ground-truth labels.

sections.heading: Uncovering physical blind spots across 17 hazard families and adversarial probes
sections.summary: The benchmark features 17 sudden event families and adversarial objects whose appearance contradicts their weight. Scenes are generated reproducibly through LLM semantic planning and seed-based physics generation, and the MLLM's motor plans are physically executed by a Unitree G1 robot inside Genesis.
sections.details:
### 3.1 The Freeze-and-Predict Protocol
At the start of an episode, a sudden hazard occurs directly in front of the virtual humanoid standing in a room—objects fall, slide, topple, or fly. The model receives initial frames spanning roughly 0.6 seconds from three synchronized cameras (first-person ego view, zoomed-in hazard view, and bird's-eye top view), capturing the onset before the outcome is determined. Time then freezes, and the model outputs a structured JSON plan containing reasoning intent, a confidence score, a planar walking velocity command (walking_cmd), and a sequence of 3D hand trajectory waypoints.

The generated plan is physically executed by a Unitree G1 humanoid inside the simulator. Crucially, the model is not asked to pick a multiple-choice token like "Catch", "Dodge", or "No_Action". Instead, the actual action is inferred via fixed rules from its walking commands and hand waypoints, preventing models from cheating by merely declaring the right answer without committing to the physical motion.

### 3.2 17 Event Families
Hazards span 17 families covering rich rigid-body mechanics: free falls, frictional slides, inverted pendulum toppling, hinged rotations, bounces, and momentum-transfer cascades. For instance, falling objects follow simple ballistic trajectories, placing higher load on semantic safety reasoning, whereas bouncing and pendulum events challenge spatiotemporal interception. Cascade reactions involve initially static objects set in motion by colliding projectiles, requiring anticipatory causal reasoning.

### 3.3 Adversarial Probes Contradicting Appearance
The benchmark includes 14 adversarial objects where visual appearance contradicts physical parameters—such as a lightweight foam anvil that looks like heavy cast iron, or a steel apple carrying high momentum despite looking like ordinary fruit. Choosing the correct reaction requires models to observe the actual initial kinematics (acceleration or deceleration) rather than relying on visual category assumptions.

### 3.4 Scene Synthesis and Ground-Truth Extraction
The pipeline operates in three stages. In Stage 1, a fixed LLM selects the event family, room, and objects from natural language prompts. In Stage 2, a deterministic RNG driven by integer seeds samples all continuous physical parameters, including initial velocities, friction, restitution, and camera poses. In Stage 3, the Genesis physics engine executes the 240 Hz rigid-body simulation, automatically logging exact ground truth such as the 3D impact coordinate $\mathbf{p}_{\text{impact}}$ passing the humanoid's reach envelope and time-to-contact.

captions.F1: Examples of the 17 sudden event families in ReactHuman. Encompassing diverse dynamics such as falling, sliding, toppling, and chain reactions, each family is designed to stress different facets of perception, causal reasoning, and motion forecasting.

sections.heading: Five diagnostic metrics to score reasonable, safe, and physically grounded reactions
sections.summary: To cleanly dissect failure modes, we designed five metrics: Semantic Action Accuracy (SAA), Safety Validity, Physical Endpoint Distance, Action-Intent Alignment (AIA), and Hand-Distance Evolution (HDE). These independently evaluate behavioral correctness, safety, and 3D spatial grounding.
sections.details:
In ReactHuman, the executed action $\hat{a}$ is derived from the model's planned walking command and hand waypoints using deterministic rules, and scored across five metrics:

- **1. Semantic Action Accuracy (SAA)**: Evaluates whether the executed action matches the ground-truth label $a^*$ ($\mathrm{SAA} = \mathbf{1}[\hat{a} = a^*]$).
- **2. Safety Validity**: A binary flag independently capturing catastrophic safety failures. An action is marked unsafe if it violates any of four rules: unparseable output (R1), attempting to catch an object designated as dangerous (R2), remaining passive in the presence of a hazard (R3), or choosing Catch or No_Action when the correct response is Dodge (R4). Even if catching is feasible, reaching for a hazardous object violates safety.
- **3. Physical Endpoint Distance**: The Euclidean distance $d_{\text{end}} = \lVert \mathbf{h}_{\text{final}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{impact}} \rVert_2$ in meters between the final hand position $\mathbf{h}_{\text{final}}$ and the true impact point $\mathbf{p}_{\text{impact}}$. Even with a correct action choice, poor 3D spatial prediction yields a high distance.
- **4. Action–Intent Alignment (AIA)**: Assesses on a 3-point scale (0, 0.5, 1) whether the model's textual intent aligns with the ground-truth behavioral goal, teasing apart motor execution errors from perceptual misunderstandings.
- **5. Hand-Distance Evolution (HDE)**: Measures the minimum distance $d_{\min}$ between the hand and the impact point across all waypoints, along with the approach delta $d_1 - d_{\min}$ from the starting position. This identifies whether the hand moved purposefully toward the target rather than drifting close by coincidence at the final frame.

sections.heading: State-of-the-art MLLMs fail one in three times: Four blind spots revealed by experiments
sections.summary: Evaluating seven MLLMs revealed that models commit safety violations in 35.9% of avoidance scenarios and exhibit extreme, fixed behavioral dispositions. Increasing model size failed to improve safety, and models proved completely unable to handle speed variations or physical properties that contradict visual appearance.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations covered seven models: five frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Kimi K2.6, Qwen3-VL-235B) and two smaller open-weight models (Qwen3-VL-30B, Gemma-3-27B). Across 306 balanced scenes sampled from the 17 families, each model received identical prompts and 0.6-second clips, yielding 2,138 physically executed decisions.

### 5.2 Key Findings and Analysis
The experiments exposed four critical vulnerabilities in current MLLMs:

- **1. Catastrophic Failures When Dodging**: In scenes where dodging was required, models violated safety rules 35.9% of the time across all evaluations. The vast majority of these errors (253 out of 392) came from freezing in place.
- **2. Fixed Dispositions Ignoring the Scene**: Six out of seven models showed an extreme bias toward retreating, fleeing even when catching was appropriate. Conversely, Claude Opus 4.8 achieved a high 67% accuracy on catch scenes but aggressively lunged at hazardous objects, dropping its accuracy in dodge scenes to just 34%. Models rely on rigid internal priors rather than adapting to observed physical dynamics.
- **3. Model Scale Does Not Guarantee Safety**: The 27B Gemma-3 model ranked second in accuracy at 62.4% and achieved the highest safety validity at 88.2%. While smaller open models outperformed massive frontier models, Claude Opus 4.8 proved the most hazardous, scoring only 64.7% on safety validity.
- **4. Severe Spatial Misses**: Even when catching was correctly chosen, the median distance between the hand and the impact point was 0.48 meters, with 89% of attempts falling short. Models rarely combined reaching with forward stepping, remaining frozen outside reaching distance in nearly half of the trials.

### Speed Insensitivity and Adversarial Probe Results
Varying hazard speeds across four tiers revealed that models perceive speed almost as a binary property ("moving or not"). In the slowest speed tier, despite clear motion, the freeze rate doubled to 42% (compared to 21% at normal speeds), failing to recognize danger. In adversarial object tests, across 280 decisions, no model questioned an object's material or mass. Models retreated frantically from a lightweight foam door and reached for heavy steel cans at the exact same rate (39%) as lightweight aluminum cans, demonstrating total reliance on semantic category priors.

sections.heading: Implications for embodied intelligence and open limitations
sections.summary: Identified weaknesses highlight the need for safety-constrained decoding and motion-grounded training on velocity and mass. At the same time, benchmark limitations such as relying on rigid-body physics and open-loop execution point toward future closed-loop extensions.
sections.details:
### Implications for Robot Deployment
The observed failure patterns were entirely invisible under standard text-based VQA evaluations. These findings provide clear roadmaps for physical robot deployment: applying safety-constrained decoding to eliminate stationary freezing defaults, fine-tuning on paired catch-and-dodge contrastive datasets to counteract behavioral bias, and explicit visual grounding to infer velocity and mass from motion trajectories rather than semantic labels.

### Limitations
ReactHuman operates under several constraints:

- **Rigid-Body Simulation Bounds**: Relying on 240 Hz rigid-body simulation in Genesis means deformable interactions like shattering glass, flowing liquids, or tearing fabrics are absent.
- **Open-Loop Evaluation**: Decisions are planned once and executed open-loop, without evaluating closed-loop visual feedback where a robot adjusts its reaching trajectory mid-flight after a bounce.
- **Model Snapshot Dependency**: Because frontier models are evaluated via remote APIs, reported performance may fluctuate as providers update model checkpoints.

sections.heading: Conclusion: An open benchmark for establishing reactive safety
sections.summary: ReactHuman shifts MLLM physical reasoning from passive question answering to active, safety-critical reactive decision-making. By uncovering severe safety blind spots that scale does not solve, the open-source benchmark provides an actionable training signal for safe embodied AI.
sections.details:
ReactHuman marks a major paradigm shift in physical reasoning evaluation, moving from passive VQA to active, safety-critical reactive decisions. Supported by 17 event families, exact simulator ground truth, adversarial probes, and five multifaceted metrics, it diagnoses not just whether a model understands physics, but whether it can act safely in a physical environment.

Extensive evaluations across seven models reveal that safety rules are broken in roughly one-third of sudden hazards, driven by rigid behavioral biases that scaling alone does not resolve. The authors have open-sourced the benchmark dataset and evaluation codebase to help the research community develop physically grounded, safety-aware embodied agents.

takeaways: Scoring high on VQA does not translate to reactive robot safety; evaluation must incorporate physical simulation and executed actions.
Scaling model parameters does not directly improve reactive safety or spatial endpoint precision, with smaller open-weight models sometimes acting more safely than frontier models.
Current MLLMs fail to perceive velocity as a continuous variable and cannot override appearance-based physical priors using observed motion dynamics.
Even when selecting the correct catch action, models fail to coordinate forward stepping with arm reaching, frequently swinging half a meter short of the target.
limitations: Evaluations use an open-loop setup planning from an initial observation window, leaving closed-loop visual trajectory correction unmeasured.
Simulation is restricted to rigid-body mechanics, excluding non-rigid hazards such as breaking glass, liquid spills, or entangled cloth.
How faithfully the simulator humanoid results transfer to physical hardware with motor latency and torque constraints remains unverified.
